Hydrogen connects orbital shape, probability flow and light through one wavefunction. Each topic starts with its defining equations; expand the derivation to follow the steps, conventions and limits of the model.

01

Three numbers, one state

Three quantum numbers identify a spatial hydrogen eigenstate. The shell nnn sets energy, ℓ\ellℓ sets angular momentum, and mmm sets its projection along the chosen axis.

Single-valued angular functions must return to themselves after a full turn: eim(φ+2π)=eimφ\mathrm e^{\mathrm im(\varphi+2\pi)}=\mathrm e^{\mathrm im\varphi}eim(φ+2π)=eimφ. Thus mmm is an integer. The angular-momentum ladder terminates at m=±ℓm=\pm\ellm=±ℓ; regular radial solutions require n≥ℓ+1n\ge\ell+1n≥ℓ+1.

gn=∑ℓ=0n−1(2ℓ+1)=2n(n−1)2+n=n2,Nn≤6=1+4+9+16+25+36=91.\begin{aligned}g_n&=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(2\ell+1)=2\frac{n(n-1)}2+n=n^2,\\N_{n\le6}&=1+4+9+16+25+36=91.\end{aligned}gn​Nn≤6​​=ℓ=0∑n−1​(2ℓ+1)=22n(n−1)​+n=n2,=1+4+9+16+25+36=91.​

For a 6f state, n=6n=6n=6, ℓ=3\ell=3ℓ=3, and mmm can take seven values, from −3-3−3 to +3+3+3. Opposite magnetic signs share a complex-state density but reverse its circulation.

02

The equation behind the cloud

A single electron in a Coulomb potential obeys the Schrödinger equation. Its normalizable bound states have discrete, negative energies that depend only on nnn.

iℏ∂Ψ∂t=[−ℏ22me∇2−e24πε0r]Ψ\mathrm i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial t}=\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla^2-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}\right]\Psiiℏ∂t∂Ψ​=[−2me​ℏ2​∇2−4πε0​re2​]Ψ
En=−ℏ22mea02n2≈−13.606  eVn2E_n=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_ea_0^2n^2}\approx-\frac{13.606\;\mathrm{eV}}{n^2}En​=−2me​a02​n2ℏ2​≈−n213.606eV​
Derivation & detailsSeparation, boundary conditions and energy

From time evolution to an energy eigenvalue

The model uses one electron and a fixed proton. Relativity, spin, external fields and electron–electron interactions are omitted.

Insert Ψ(r,t)=ψ(r)e−iEt/ℏ\Psi(\mathbf r,t)=\psi(\mathbf r)\mathrm e^{-\mathrm iEt/\hbar}Ψ(r,t)=ψ(r)e−iEt/ℏ. The time derivative contributes EEE, leaving a time-independent eigenvalue equation. Separating its angular part gives the radial equation:

H^ψ=Eψ,−ℏ22me[1r2ddr(r2dRdr)−ℓ(ℓ+1)r2R]−e24πε0rR=ER.\begin{aligned}\hat H\psi&=E\psi,\\-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\left[\frac1{r^2}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dr}\left(r^2\frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dr}\right)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}R\right]-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}R&=ER.\end{aligned}H^ψ−2me​ℏ2​[r21​drd​(r2drdR​)−r2ℓ(ℓ+1)​R]−4πε0​re2​R​=Eψ,=ER.​

A bound solution must remain regular at the origin and decay at infinity. After extracting rℓr^\ellrℓ and the exponential tail, the remaining series must terminate; its polynomial degree is n−ℓ−1n-\ell-1n−ℓ−1. That condition produces the discrete energy spectrum. The minus sign means that energy must be supplied to reach the free-electron threshold E=0E=0E=0.

Complex spherical harmonics have a winding phase. Real orbitals combine opposite magnetic states to form directional lobes; both describe bases of the same state space.

Complex basis

Phase winds mmm times around zzz. Opposite mmm values have identical densities and opposite current. The global time phase changes no probabilities.

Real basis

Combine ±q\pm q±q to make the familiar directional lobes. The signed index selects cosine (+)(+)(+) or sine (−)(- )(−), rather than a definite LzL_zLz​.

Real orbitals have ℓ\ellℓ angular nodal surfaces. Complex orbitals have ℓ−∣m∣\ell-|m|ℓ−∣m∣ polar nodal surfaces, with an additional zero on the zzz axis when ∣m∣>0|m|>0∣m∣>0. NIST DLMF · Spherical harmonics ↗

06

What the moving particles mean

A cloud can remain stationary while probability circulates. Current depends on the spatial phase gradient; the tracers visualize that flow rather than measured electron paths.

v=jρ=ℏmmersin⁡θ e^φ\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf j}{\rho}=\frac{\hbar m}{m_er\sin\theta}\,\hat{\mathbf e}_\varphiv=ρj​=me​rsinθℏm​e^φ​
Derivation & detailsContinuity equation and the phase gradient

Deriving conservation and circulation

Differentiate ρ=Ψ∗Ψ\rho=\Psi^*\Psiρ=Ψ∗Ψ, insert the Schrödinger equation and its complex conjugate, and subtract. A real potential cancels; the kinetic terms combine into a divergence:

∂tρ=iℏ2me∇ ⁣⋅(Ψ∗∇Ψ−Ψ∇Ψ∗)=−∇ ⁣⋅j.\partial_t\rho=\frac{\mathrm i\hbar}{2m_e}\nabla\!\cdot\left(\Psi^*\nabla\Psi-\Psi\nabla\Psi^*\right)=-\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf j.∂t​ρ=2me​iℏ​∇⋅(Ψ∗∇Ψ−Ψ∇Ψ∗)=−∇⋅j.

Writing Ψ=ρ eiS/ℏ\Psi=\sqrt\rho\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm iS/\hbar}Ψ=ρ​eiS/ℏ gives j=ρ∇S/me\mathbf j=\rho\nabla S/m_ej=ρ∇S/me​. For an eigenstate, S=mℏφ−EntS=m\hbar\varphi-E_ntS=mℏφ−En​t; using ∇φ=e^φ/(rsin⁡θ)\nabla\varphi=\hat{\mathbf e}_\varphi/(r\sin\theta)∇φ=e^φ​/(rsinθ) gives the displayed flow velocity. Dividing that tangential speed by rsin⁡θr\sin\thetarsinθ yields its angular speed.

Angular motion and its limits

For a complex hydrogen eigenstate, the azimuthal velocity gives these coordinate rates away from nodes:

dφdt=ℏmmer2sin⁡2θ,drdt=dθdt=0\frac{\mathrm d\varphi}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\hbar m}{m_er^2\sin^2\theta},\qquad\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt}=0dtdφ​=me​r2sin2θℏm​,dtdr​=dtdθ​=0

Changing the sign of mmm reverses circulation. For m=0m=0m=0, or a stationary real orbital, the current is zero. A stationary cloud can therefore have a circulating current while its density stays constant.

Tracers illustrate this flow field; they are not measured electron trajectories. Animation time is rescaled for visibility and is not a laboratory clock. At a node, j/ρ\mathbf j/\rhoj/ρ is undefined. MIT · Probability current and conservation ↗

07

From mathematics to the screen

The renderer maps density to brightness and phase to hue. Cloud integrates a volume; Granular displays samples from that same probability distribution.

ρ(r)=∣ψ(r)∣2,ϕ(r)=arg⁡ψ(r)\rho(\mathbf r)=|\psi(\mathbf r)|^2,\qquad \phi(\mathbf r)=\arg\psi(\mathbf r)ρ(r)=∣ψ(r)∣2,ϕ(r)=argψ(r)
Derivation & detailsSampling, color and rendering limits

What sampling estimates

For normalized density, an independent sample lands in a region VVV with probability P(V)P(V)P(V). A collection of NNN samples therefore has expected regional count

E[NV]=N∫Vρ(r) d3r.\mathbb E[N_V]=N\int_V\rho(\mathbf r)\,\mathrm d^3\mathbf r.E[NV​]=N∫V​ρ(r)d3r.

Increasing the sample count reveals finer structure without changing the underlying state. Color and exposure make that structure legible: they are display choices, not another physical observable. The finite volume and finite number of samples approximate the analytic distribution.

Visual mappings and sampling limits

The renderer evaluates the analytic orbital in three dimensions, then accumulates samples along viewing rays. Density mode uses brightness to expose structure; the single-orbital phase view colors the complex angle arg⁡Ψ\arg\PsiargΨ. Density keeps its blue-to-white palette. Phase uses a vibrant cyclic rainbow. The colors at −π-\pi−π and +π+\pi+π match, and hue transitions remain smooth as the angle wraps around a full turn. In phase mode, hue represents an angle, not a probability.

Shading is a visual mapping

State-dependent exposure and nonlinear brightness reveal faint outer lobes. Display brightness is not an absolute probability scale, and equal brightness across different orbitals does not imply equal density.

Granular particles add depth

Each probability sample is a softly shaded matte sphere with depth testing. Density shading uses dark blue through pale blue and white. These spheres are probability samples, not solid electrons or emitted light. Cloud mode emphasizes the integrated density; Granular emphasizes the individual samples.

Tracer limits

Cloud and Granular remember separate tracer ceilings. Selecting Real in Cloud starts with zero tracers; Complex starts with 5,000, and either can then be adjusted. Granular starts with 200,000. Each style remembers its intensity, flow speed, cut settings, auto rotation and axes independently. Basis and Density/Phase are shared across styles. The main explorer starts in Granular with a wedge; the transition viewer retains Whole as its Granular default. Granular intensity and flow speed both default to 2. Flow speed snaps to ¼×, ½×, 1×, 2× or 4×. Its control is shown only for Complex; flow runs continuously. The tracer slider sets the maximum requested samples for that style, up to 10,000 in Cloud and 200,000 in Granular. A background limiter lowers the active count rapidly when measured frame rate falls below the target, then restores samples when there is sustained headroom, never exceeding the slider setting. Granular targets 30 FPS in both viewers and keeps its raster resolution fixed. Cloud retains adaptive resolution and targets 30 FPS in the orbital explorer and 60 FPS in the transition viewer. The active count is shown when limited. Volume sampling and pixel resolution also cost GPU time. These frame rates are performance goals, not guarantees or physical oscillation frequencies. Hidden and stationary views do not drive upward adjustments.

Cutaways reveal existing structure

Half, wedge and slice controls hide parts of the rendered volume. They do not collapse, renormalize or physically change the quantum state.

Sampling changes visual detail

More ray steps and pixels improve detail; more tracers sample the same flow. Finite viewing bounds omit diffuse outer tails, a soft edge fade avoids a visible cutoff, and finite sampling can soften narrow nodes.

08

One wavelength, many state pairs

One spectral line fixes an energy gap, not a unique pair of orbital shapes. In the displayed hydrogen model, 15 shell pairs give 15 distinct wavelengths.

En=−13.605693 eVn2,ΔEab=13.605693 eV(1a2−1b2),λab=hcΔEab,hc=1239.841984332 eV nm.\begin{aligned}E_n&=-\frac{13.605693\,\mathrm{eV}}{n^2},\\[0.5em]\Delta E_{ab}&=13.605693\,\mathrm{eV}\left(\frac{1}{a^2}-\frac{1}{b^2}\right),\\[0.5em]\lambda_{ab}&=\frac{hc}{\Delta E_{ab}},\qquad hc=1239.841984332\,\mathrm{eV\,nm}.\end{aligned}En​ΔEab​λab​​=−n213.605693eV​,=13.605693eV(a21​−b21​),=ΔEab​hc​,hc=1239.841984332eVnm.​
Nlines=(62)=15N_{\mathrm{lines}}=\binom{6}{2}=15Nlines​=(26​)=15
Derivation & detailsRydberg relation and complete pair counts

Energy difference to wavelength

Subtract the two bound-state energies and equate the result to a photon’s hν=hc/λh\nu=hc/\lambdahν=hc/λ. The lower shell has the more negative energy, so Eb−Ea>0E_b-E_a>0Eb​−Ea​>0 for b>ab>ab>a.

1λab=13.605693 eVhc(1a2−1b2).\frac1{\lambda_{ab}}=\frac{13.605693\,\mathrm{eV}}{hc}\left(\frac1{a^2}-\frac1{b^2}\right).λab​1​=hc13.605693eV​(a21​−b21​).

For a=2a=2a=2, b=3b=3b=3, the gap is approximately 1.890 eV1.890\,\mathrm{eV}1.890eV, giving a model vacuum wavelength near 656.1 nm656.1\,\mathrm{nm}656.1nm. All allowed orbital pairs between those shells share that gap. Counting shell pairs gives 6⋅5/2=156\cdot5/2=156⋅5/2=15; counting magnetic channels additionally requires the angular selection rules.

Shell degeneracy and spectral series

gn=∑ℓ=0n−1(2ℓ+1)=n2,∑n=16n2=91g_n=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(2\ell+1)=n^2,\qquad\sum_{n=1}^{6}n^2=91gn​=ℓ=0∑n−1​(2ℓ+1)=n2,n=1∑6​n2=91

Let a=nlowera=n_{\mathrm{lower}}a=nlower​ and b=nupperb=n_{\mathrm{upper}}b=nupper​, with a<ba\lt ba<b. These shell indices identify the positive gap and vacuum wavelength in the main equation.

The 15 shell pairs through n=6n=6n=6 have 15 distinct gaps. Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund end at a=1,2,3,4,5a=1,2,3,4,5a=1,2,3,4,5, respectively. The spectrum stops at n=6n=6n=6; each physical series continues beyond the displayed lines toward its series limit.

A fixed Δn=b−a\Delta n=b-aΔn=b−a groups several wavelengths; it does not determine a wavelength. For example, 1↔21\leftrightarrow21↔2 and 5↔65\leftrightarrow65↔6 both change nnn by one, but have very different gaps. A selected wavelength identifies the shell pair, then the subshell and magnetic-channel controls identify its spatial states.

Counting the allowed pairs

For a fixed a<ba\lt ba<b, the electric-dipole rule Δℓ=±1\Delta\ell=\pm1Δℓ=±1 permits aaa upward-ℓ\ellℓ branches and a−1a-1a−1 downward-ℓ\ellℓ branches. A branch connecting ℓ\ellℓ and ℓ+1\ell+1ℓ+1 contains 3(2ℓ+1)3(2\ell+1)3(2ℓ+1) magnetic channels, one for every allowed lower mmm and q=0,±1q=0,\pm1q=0,±1.

Selection rules, polarization and coupling

Electric-dipole selection rules identify allowed pairs. Their matrix elements determine coupling strength; a nonzero coupling is not a transition probability.

Derivation & detailsSelection rules, angular overlap and strength

Why the dipole rules follow

In the long-wavelength approximation, the electron’s dipole is d^=−er\hat{\mathbf d}=-e\mathbf rd^=−er, with interaction H^′=−d^⋅E(t)\hat H'= -\hat{\mathbf d}\cdot\mathbf E(t)H^′=−d^⋅E(t). Multiplying a position-operator component by −e-e−e gives the corresponding dipole component.

The azimuthal part of the angular overlap contains ei(m+q−M)φ\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(m+q-M)\varphi}ei(m+q−M)φ. Its integral over a full turn is zero unless M=m+qM=m+qM=m+q. The rank-one dipole has q=0,±1q=0,\pm1q=0,±1, giving ∣Δm∣≤1|\Delta m|\le1∣Δm∣≤1.

The odd parity of r\mathbf rr requires opposite parities for the two states, excluding L=ℓL=\ellL=ℓ and leaving Δℓ=±1\Delta\ell=\pm1Δℓ=±1. Separating radial and angular factors then turns the squared dipole amplitude into the strength ScS_cSc​ in the main equation.

Magnetic-sign symmetry

Simultaneously reversing both magnetic numbers preserves the complex-state densities and dipole strength while reversing their probability currents: (m,M,q)↦(−m,−M,−q)(m,M,q)\mapsto(-m,-M,-q)(m,M,q)↦(−m,−M,−q). The sign selector σ=±1\sigma=\pm1σ=±1 switches these partners.

Here q=Δm=M−mq=\Delta m=M-mq=Δm=M−m. The magnetic-change controls choose ∣Δm∣=0|\Delta m|=0∣Δm∣=0 or ∣Δm∣=1|\Delta m|=1∣Δm∣=1. For ∣Δm∣=1|\Delta m|=1∣Δm∣=1, the table uses the q=+1q=+1q=+1 reference pairs. The negative sign reverses both reference magnetic numbers and gives physical q=−1q=-1q=−1; the cards, their order and selection stay fixed, while their displayed magnetic signs update to the actual states. For ∣Δm∣=0|\Delta m|=0∣Δm∣=0, the table uses nonnegative magnetic representatives. Only changing the magnetic-change magnitude changes the table. This groups symmetry partners without discarding physical channels.

The + button uses the reference pair, not necessarily two positive magnetic numbers. For example, 5p,−1↔6s,05p,-1\leftrightarrow6s,05p,−1↔6s,0 has reference q=+1q=+1q=+1; reversing both signs gives 5p,+1↔6s,05p,+1\leftrightarrow6s,05p,+1↔6s,0 with q=−1q=-1q=−1. An s orbital always has m=0m=0m=0. The animation labels show the actual signed states. For two zero magnetic numbers, both sign choices represent the same channel.

Across all 15 lines, 260 symmetry-grouped cards represent 465 signed channels; the 55 zero-to-zero channels are counted only once. A selected-orbital filter can exclude a reversed partner; clear that filter to access it.

What dipole strength means

The readout measures the squared spatial dipole matrix element. The relative value is normalized against the strongest magnetic channel on the same wavelength, including all subshells and all three polarization components.

ScS_cSc​ has units of a02a_0^2a02​; multiplying it by e2e^2e2 gives the squared electric-dipole moment. Filters do not change the denominator. A relative value of one identifies the strongest channel at that wavelength; it is not a 100% transition probability.

Observed line brightness also depends on the number of atoms in each state, the illuminating field, polarization, frequency, decay and observation geometry. Spontaneous-emission rates scale as ω3\omega^3ω3 times dipole strength; emitted power also includes photon energy and upper-state population. Summing channels requires a specified population model. The spectrum therefore presents coupling strengths, not predicted measured intensities.

Driven motion between two states

A resonant drive exchanges population between an isolated pair of states. The animation keeps that slow exchange and averages over the much faster optical oscillation.

Solving the resonant two-state problem

Choose the drive phase so the resonant rotating-frame coupling is real. With the atom initially in the lower state, the effective equations are

iddt(clcu)=Ω2(0110)(clcu),(cl(0)cu(0))=(10).\mathrm i\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\begin{pmatrix}c_l\\c_u\end{pmatrix}=\frac\Omega2\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c_l\\c_u\end{pmatrix},\qquad\begin{pmatrix}c_l(0)\\c_u(0)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.idtd​(cl​cu​​)=2Ω​(01​10​)(cl​cu​​),(cl​(0)cu​(0)​)=(10​).

Differentiating once more gives c¨l=−(Ω/2)2cl\ddot c_l=-(\Omega/2)^2c_lc¨l​=−(Ω/2)2cl​. Thus cl=cos⁡(Ωt/2)c_l=\cos(\Omega t/2)cl​=cos(Ωt/2), cu=−isin⁡(Ωt/2)c_u=-\mathrm i\sin(\Omega t/2)cu​=−isin(Ωt/2), and taking squared magnitudes gives the population cycle. Its period is 2π/Ω2\pi/\Omega2π/Ω, distinct from the optical period 2π/ω2\pi/\omega2π/ω.

Expanding the coherent density gives two population terms and an interference term. Averaging over many optical cycles removes the rapidly varying cross term, leaving the displayed mixture while preserving total probability.

Driving field and visual time

For a monochromatic field E(t)=Re⁡[E e−iωt]\mathbf E(t)=\operatorname{Re}[\boldsymbol{\mathcal E}\,\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\omega t}]E(t)=Re[Ee−iωt], define Ω=∣⟨u∣d^⋅E∣l⟩∣/ℏ\Omega=|\langle u|\hat{\mathbf d}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mathcal E}|l\rangle|/\hbarΩ=∣⟨u∣d^⋅E∣l⟩∣/ℏ. Thus physical Rabi rates depend on field amplitude, polarization and the channel's dipole matrix element. With one matched field component held fixed, Ω\OmegaΩ scales as Sc\sqrt{S_c}Sc​​.

The display defaults to a 1.25-second cycle

The transition-speed control scales the visual cycle in five steps: 1/4×, 1/2×, 1×, 2× and 4× (5 to 0.3125 seconds), independently of circulation speed. This visual timing makes different shapes easy to compare and does not predict physical Rabi times or scale playback by dipole strength. Each descriptor’s border brightens toward white as its population grows. The rising upper-state population illustrates absorption; the falling population illustrates stimulated emission. The repeating animation is not repeated spontaneous decay.

The coherent wavefunction contains two energy-dependent phases:

Its density has an interference term oscillating at the optical difference frequency. The transition cloud averages over that fast oscillation while retaining the slow populations:

The averaging assumes an interval long compared with the optical period and short compared with the population cycle. The two normalized distributions share one physical coordinate scale; a common visual exposure is applied after mixing. Both probabilities add to one, and the integrated density remains one.

Every selected channel uses the complex magnetic basis ∣n,ℓ,m⟩|n,\ell,m\rangle∣n,ℓ,m⟩. Opposite signs of mmm have identical density, so some different channels look the same in this averaged view even though their phase, current or polarization coupling differs. The state labels and dipole-strength readout retain that distinction. The atlas's real orbitals are superpositions of the complex states, not additional channels to be added to the count.

Two-state scope

With degenerate magnetic sublevels, a real applied field can couple several states simultaneously. This view isolates one matrix element at a time; a wavelength alone does not prepare a unique channel. It omits multilevel coherent dynamics, spontaneous decay, decoherence, saturation in an ensemble and line broadening. Electric-quadrupole, magnetic-dipole, multiphoton and ionization processes are outside this electric-dipole, bound-state model. A dipole-forbidden transition can still occur by another mechanism.

Visible spectral colors are approximate; ultraviolet and infrared lines use blue interface markers, not visible photon colors. Each orbital card is a density cross section scaled independently to its own radius and peak density; the animated pair shares one spatial scale. The orbital cloud is a probability distribution; it does not depict an electron traveling between two surfaces. MIT · Coherently driven two-level systems ↗

Viewing a transition: basis, phase and current

The transition preview separates basis choice, phase color and component circulation. These are views of the selected energy shells, while the reported coupling refers to the selected complex states.

Transform amplitudes before taking their magnitude

A real endpoint is a normalized linear combination of complex magnetic states. If ∣l′⟩=∑m∣l,m⟩(Ul)ml′|l'\rangle=\sum_m|l,m\rangle(U_l)_{ml'}∣l′⟩=∑m​∣l,m⟩(Ul​)ml′​, and similarly for the upper state, inserting both expansions into ⟨u′∣rq∣l′⟩\langle u'|r_q|l'\rangle⟨u′∣rq​∣l′⟩ gives Uu†D(q)UlU_u^\dagger D^{(q)}U_lUu†​D(q)Ul​.

The order matters: amplitudes can interfere, so transforming a table of already-squared strengths generally gives a different result. The real preview preserves shell energies and visualizes the alternative shapes; it does not recompute a physical drive between those real combinations.

Likewise, the weighted circulation overlay is not the full transport current during population transfer. Taking the time derivative of the averaged density exposes the missing transfer term, derived below.

Interpreting the transition preview

Complex states and real-basis previews

Complex mode displays the two magnetic eigenstates named by the selected channel. Real mode replaces each endpoint by its normalized real counterpart from section 04: the positive index selects a cosine combination, the negative index a sine combination. This is a preview of different basis shapes in the same energy shells, not a claim that their coupling equals the selected complex channel's coupling.

The wavelength is unchanged because these combinations have the same shell energies. The displayed selection rules, polarization and strength continue to refer to the named complex states. A physical transition calculation between real combinations would transform the full matrix of dipole amplitudes before taking its squared magnitude:

The columns of UlU_lUl​ and UuU_uUu​ contain the real basis vectors expressed in their complex magnetic bases. The signed index in a real preview is not a definite value of angular momentum along zzz. Real combinations add no independent states to the catalog.

Component phase is a color convention

After optical averaging, the density is a population-weighted sum. This averaged representation has no unique single wavefunction phase to color; it does not assert that the underlying driven state has physically decohered. The cloud therefore colors each component's phase separately, then blends its colors according to local density. With pl=1−Pp_l=1-Ppl​=1−P, pu=Pp_u=Ppu​=P, ρk=∣ψk∣2\rho_k=|\psi_k|^2ρk​=∣ψk​∣2, and a cyclic color map FFF, the unshaded volume color is

Here ϕk\phi_kϕk​ is the phase of one component in the display's chosen convention; each component particle carries its own phase color. Zero-density regions contribute no color. The palette wraps smoothly at −π-\pi−π and +π+\pi+π. Blended colors are not the phase of a coherent superposition and do not restore the interference term omitted in section 10. Changing a component's arbitrary overall phase changes its colors without changing its density or coupling strength.

Circulation is separate from population transfer

The tracers sample each endpoint distribution and circle according to that component's stationary current. Their population weights change with the cycle. They illustrate the component circulation field

jcirc=(1−P)jl+Pju,jk=ℏmeIm⁡ ⁣(ψk∗∇ψk).\mathbf j_{\mathrm{circ}}=(1-P)\mathbf j_l+P\mathbf j_u,\qquad\mathbf j_k=\frac{\hbar}{m_e}\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\psi_k^*\nabla\psi_k\right).jcirc​=(1−P)jl​+Pju​,jk​=me​ℏ​Im(ψk∗​∇ψk​).

Each stationary complex component follows the azimuthal flow in section 06. Opposite magnetic signs circulate in opposite directions. A stationary real component, or a component with m=0m=0m=0, has zero circulation. The moving samples do not travel from one orbital to the other.

This overlay does not solve the full local probability transport of the driven atom. The distinction can be seen directly: each stationary current is divergence-free, whereas the chosen population interpolation changes the local density, giving

∂ρˉ∂t+∇ ⁣⋅jcirc=P˙(ρu−ρl).\frac{\partial\bar\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf j_{\mathrm{circ}}=\dot P\left(\rho_u-\rho_l\right).∂t∂ρˉ​​+∇⋅jcirc​=P˙(ρu​−ρl​).

The right-hand side integrates to zero because both endpoint densities are normalized. It records the change of the displayed component weights; it is not creation or loss of an electron. The full driven quantum evolution conserves probability locally, but its transfer current and fast coherences are outside this averaged visualization. The circulation overlay alone must not be interpreted as that full current.

Two independent visual clocks

The transition-speed control sets the absorption–stimulated-emission cycle. Flow speed sets the illustrative circulation and phase-color clock independently of transition speed. These clocks are rescaled for viewing and do not measure physical transition times or relative optical phase.

Reading the atlas and spectrum

The atlas thumbnails show cross sections of complex-state probability density. Each thumbnail is scaled to its own radius and peak density so its structure is visible; thumbnail brightness and size are not a common quantitative scale. Opposite magnetic signs have the same complex-state density and opposite circulation. The magnetic-number buttons filter transition subsets by the magnitude of the change in magnetic number and by sign; reversing the sign reverses both endpoint magnetic numbers. For zero magnetic change the endpoints share the same magnetic number. States with zero magnetic number have no stationary circulation.

Spectral positions use vacuum wavelengths. The all-lines view uses a logarithmic wavelength axis to span the full range, while each individual series uses a linear axis.

The transition animation shows driven population transfer through optical-cycle-averaged density. Its endpoints use the same spatial scale, unlike the independently scaled atlas thumbnails. The adjustable visual cycle is slowed for inspection and is not the optical oscillation period or a measured transition lifetime.

Geometry and lighting

Granular uses softly lit matte spheres. Cloud integrates the mixed density along viewing rays. Both sample the same optical-cycle-averaged distribution. Sphere sizes and highlights aid depth perception; they are not electron sizes or emitted light. Half, wedge and slice controls hide geometry without changing or renormalizing either state. Rotation, zoom, coordinate axes and the tracer limiter affect the view, not the spectrum or coupling.

Component samples

For upper-state population PPP, the active sample budget is divided between the two normalized endpoint distributions:

Nl≈(1−P)Nactive,Nu≈PNactive.N_l\approx(1-P)N_{\mathrm{active}},\qquad N_u\approx P N_{\mathrm{active}}.Nl​≈(1−P)Nactive​,Nu​≈PNactive​.

Both components share the density palette. Equal populations mean equal sample shares, not identical silhouettes or brightness at every point. Phase mode retains its cyclic rainbow.
